issues.description: The text states 45 began training, 5 were excluded for training performance, leaving 40. The analysis then reports 'an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded).' Forty minus five equals 35, not 23, so the reported exclusion count is incompatible with the inclusion count. The actual number excluded for too-few high-confidence trials appears to be 17, not 5, meaning roughly 43% of the training-qualified sample was dropped. This discrepancy makes it impossible to know the true analyzed sample and the true attrition rate.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.description: The confidence scale for Experiment 1 is reported inconsistently. The procedure text states a 2-point scale ('one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain)'), while the Figure 1 caption states a 4-point scale ('1 = guess, 4 = certainty'). These cannot both be true, and the difference is material because the definition of 'high confidence' trials—the central dependent measure—depends entirely on the scale used.
issues.quote: After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain).

issues.description: The entire analytic strategy hinges on isolating 'high confidence' trials, yet the manuscript never defines what scale value(s) count as high confidence on the 1-4 scale used in Experiments 2-4 (e.g., only 4, or 3 and 4). Without this threshold the central analyses cannot be replicated or evaluated, and the cross-experiment comparability of 'high confidence' is unknown (especially given the apparent 2-point scale in Experiment 1).
issues.quote: As in Experiment 1, error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), memory delay (long or short) and error type

issues.description: Across experiments, very large fractions of participants were excluded for having too few high-confidence trials per cell (e.g., 92/290 ≈ 32% in Experiment 2). Because exclusion is based on a variable (rate of high-confidence responding) plausibly correlated with the outcome (propensity to make confident illusory reports), this selective exclusion can bias the estimated illusion rates. Excluded participants differ systematically (e.g., 15.7% vs 49.2% high-confidence trials in Exp 2), confirming the groups are not exchangeable.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions.

issues.subcategory: failed manipulation interpreted as theoretical result
issues.description: The cue-color manipulation in Experiment 2 produced no effect, and the post-experiment questionnaire showed no participant detected the cue-target contingency. This indicates the implicit expectation was likely never learned (a failed/ineffective manipulation), so the null result cannot support the theoretical claim that 'expectations need substantial time to develop.' A manipulation that participants never internalized cannot adjudicate whether transient expectations can shape memory.
issues.quote: However, transiently generated expectations, in this case provided by a cue about the prevalence of real versus pseudo-letters targets, had no effect on the prevalence of illusory memories. This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories.

issues.description: The discussion asserts that 'all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories,' but the authors explicitly state they did not test iconic memory and that iconic memory is sometimes thought to be immune to such biases. The strong claim contradicts the acknowledged scope of the data (only WM- and FM-like conditions were tested).
issues.quote: The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research

issues.subcategory: trace-rewriting claim not distinguishable from retrieval-time inference
issues.description: The authors interpret the increase in illusions over time as evidence that 'correctly encoded percepts...are being converted to illusory memories,' i.e., that the stored trace is overwritten. However, an increase in confident errors as the trace weakens is equally consistent with reconstruction/inference occurring at the moment of retrieval (priors filling a degraded trace), without any change to a stored representation. The data cannot distinguish online trace transformation from retrieval-stage inference, so the 'reshaping the memory trace' causal claim is overstated.
issues.quote: Over time illusions become more prevalent, indicating that correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter.

issues.description: Pseudo-letters can be spontaneously recoded into their canonical verbal label (seeing 'Ɔ' but encoding the name 'C'), so the asymmetric pseudo-to-real errors may reflect a verbal labeling/encoding strategy rather than a genuine reshaping of a visual memory representation by 'world knowledge.' No articulatory suppression or non-verbalizable control was used to rule this out; the authors only raise it speculatively as future work, leaving the core construct (visual STM illusion vs. verbal recoding) ambiguous.
issues.quote: It is worthwhile to test, in future research, whether more decayed memory traces for real letters are similarly sensitive to memory illusions (real-to-pseudo) as pseudo-letter representations are in our experiments.

issues.subcategory: unequal response options bias illusion vs other-error comparison
issues.description: The key contrast is 'illusions' (selecting the single mirrored counterpart) versus 'other errors' (selecting any of several unrelated distractors). Because the illusion can be committed for only one response option while other errors span multiple options, the two error categories have different baseline opportunities and are not directly comparable without normalizing per option. The conclusion that illusions are 'much more prevalent than other errors' is confounded by this asymmetry in the number of eligible options.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 1 was supported: Illusions (pseudo-to-real or real-to-pseudo) were much more prevalent than other errors (a main effect of Error Type, BFincl>1000).

issues.subcategory: WEIRD, sex-skewed, literate-only sample and stimulus class
issues.description: Samples are young (mean ~20), predominantly female (e.g., 51/64 women in Exp 3; 164/290 in Exp 2) first-year psychology students, and the stimuli are alphabetic letters requiring literacy. The conclusions are framed broadly ('memory is shaped by what we expected to see,' implications for vision research generally), but the narrow sample and a single overlearned stimulus category limit generalization to memory in general, other populations, and non-letter stimuli. These limitations are not acknowledged.
issues.quote: Thus, it seems that short-term memory is not always an accurate representation of what was just perceived. Instead, memory is shaped by what we expected to see, right from the formation of the first memory trace.

issues.description: Experiment 4 was run online on participants' own laptops via Zoom, yet stimuli are specified in precise degrees of visual angle and brief durations (250 ms displays, 500 ms intervals). Online administration cannot guarantee viewing distance, display size/calibration, or millisecond timing accuracy, undermining the stimulus specifications and the comparability of the time-course manipulation with the lab-based experiments.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting . Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time.

issues.description: The sentence describes a 5% difference as a 'smaller increase' than a 4% difference, which is internally contradictory (5% is larger than 4%). This makes the reported direction/magnitude of the target-type by memory-delay pattern for illusions uninterpretable as written.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.description: The Experiment 4 results refer to 'Figure 5,' but Figure 5 is the Experiment 3 figure; the Experiment 4 data are in Figure 6. This mislabeling impedes correct reading of the results.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used optional-stopping sequential Bayesian designs with different decision thresholds (BF of 6 vs BF of 10) and a periodic checking schedule, without justification for the threshold choice or evidence of pre-registration. Differing, unjustified stopping rules across nominally similar experiments constitute researcher degrees of freedom that can inflate evidential strength.
issues.quote: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop.

issues.description: The interpretive thresholds are mislabeled relative to conventional schemes: BF between 0.33 and 1 is labeled 'substantial evidence for the null' when it is conventionally only anecdotal/weak, and BF < 0.33 is labeled 'strong' when 0.1-0.33 is typically 'moderate.' These nonstandard labels can overstate the strength of null and alternative evidence throughout.
issues.quote: Bayes Factors were interpreted as follows: BF < 0.33: strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33 - 1: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis.

issues.description: Error-rate proportions—bounded at 0-1 and with several cells near the floor (e.g., 4-7% other errors)—are analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA, which assumes approximately normal, homoscedastic residuals. Skewed, floor-bounded proportions violate these assumptions; a model appropriate for proportions/counts (e.g., binomial GLMM) would be more defensible. No assumption checks are reported.
issues.quote: relative occurrence of high confidence selection as the dependent variable.

issues.description: Participants received accuracy feedback after every trial (and block-level accuracy feedback). Because feedback signals when a confident pseudo-to-real response was wrong, it could train participants to reduce illusions over the session or otherwise alter response strategy, confounding the time-course interpretation. No analysis of practice/learning across blocks is reported to address this.
issues.quote: They were instructed to select "none of these" if the target letter was not a response option. After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 target proportion not reconciled with cue probabilities
issues.description: The General Discussion states pseudo-letters were 33% of targets in Experiment 2, but the design specifies 25% pseudo targets on red-cue trials and 60% on blue-cue trials. A 33% overall rate requires a specific (unreported) ratio of red to blue trials (~77% red). The proportion of red versus blue trials is never stated, which is needed both to verify the 33% figure and to evaluate the strength of the implicit expectation manipulation.
issues.quote: with pseudo-letters making up 25% (Experiment 1) and 33% (Experiment 2) of the targets, while real letters were the target in the remainder of trials.

issues.subcategory: time and interference confounded in Experiment 1
issues.description: Experiment 1 collapses 'longer memory delay' and 'visual interference' into a single notion of memory deterioration, and the conditions differ simultaneously in delay, presence/timing of the interfering display, and the moment of report. Because the Short-with-interference and Long conditions differ from Short on multiple dimensions at once, the unique contributions of time versus interference cannot be isolated, weakening the claim that decay/interference per se drives the increase.
issues.quote: as memory deteriorates with a larger memory delay or more visual interference, the increase in illusory errors (7% increase from 19% in the short delay to 26% averaged over the short with interference and long delay) is larger than other errors

issues.description: In Experiment 1 the authors dismiss a response-bias explanation by asserting the pattern is 'consistent with memory-driven processes,' but provide no analysis or evidence in Experiment 1 to actually distinguish a response bias from a memory effect. The claim is circular and the bias was only later addressed in Experiment 3 via the balanced set; the Experiment 1 assertion is unsupported.
issues.quote: However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.description: The three-way interaction in Experiment 1 has only anecdotal support (BFincl = 2.45), yet the authors interpret its pattern substantively (e.g., a specific 12% increase for pseudo-letter targets). Interpreting effects the analysis itself flags as anecdotal risks over-reading noise.
issues.quote: Finally, there is only anecdotal evidence for a three-way interaction between Target Type, Error Type and Memory Delay (BFincl = 2.45): For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase 12% as memory deteriorates through interference of time or visual information (29% illusions to 41% illusions).

issues.subcategory: set size not analyzed and collapsed without justification
issues.description: Experiment 1 used memory displays of 6 or 8 letters with differing numbers of pseudo-letters, but set size is never entered as a factor; results are simply 'averaged across the set size conditions.' Because set size affects memory load and the number of critical trials per cell, collapsing it without analysis hides a potential moderator and affects the per-cell trial counts driving exclusions.
issues.quote: resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: no power analysis or a priori sample justification for Exps 1-2
issues.description: Experiment 1's sample size is not justified by any power/precision analysis, and Experiment 2's sample is determined entirely by course enrollment. Combined with the very small number of critical high-confidence trials per cell (~13% of trials are critical, further split by delay, target type, and confidence), several subgroup cells are likely underpowered, which is also why so many participants fell below the inclusion threshold.
issues.quote: The number of participants was determined not by the experimenter but by student enrollment in the course, which explains the large increase in participants compared to Experiment 1.

issues.subcategory: mislabeling interference condition as a WM manipulation
issues.description: The authors classify the cue-with-interference condition as 'a trial-type most like a WM manipulation' and infer that illusions occur in working memory, but presenting interference at the cue does not operationally define working memory (which concerns active maintenance/manipulation, not merely concurrent distraction). This loose mapping of conditions onto IM/WM/FM stages overstates which memory subsystems were tested.
issues.quote: Experiment 1 shows that when the memory cue is presented together with unrelated information, a trial-type most like a WM manipulation, illusory memories are highly prevalent.

issues.subcategory: key model-comparison details deferred to unavailable appendix
issues.description: All full model comparisons are deferred to 'Appendix 1,' which is not provided, and BFm is reported for selected best models without the full posterior model probabilities. Readers cannot evaluate the robustness of model selection (e.g., closeness of competing models) or the sensitivity to prior choices in the Bayesian ANOVA.
issues.quote: had the best fit (BFm = 18, see Appendix 1 for full model comparison and Table 1 for an overview of BFincl for each model component).

issues.subcategory: high confidence assumed to index genuine memory rather than metacognitive error
issues.description: The inferential logic treats high-confidence errors as proof of an 'actual, albeit false, memory' and excludes guessing by construction. But high confidence can itself be an erroneous metacognitive judgment (overconfidence), so confident errors do not necessarily reflect access to a (false) memory trace rather than confidently endorsed inference. This assumption underlies the central interpretation and is asserted rather than validated.
issues.quote: Therefore, isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.
